## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1975_FA_Cup_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

This was the second time that West Ham United had won the FA Cup. As defending champions the [following season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_FA_Cup "1975–76 FA Cup"), they were eliminated at the first hurdle after losing 2–0 to [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") at Upton Park in the third round. They would win the FA Cup for a third time in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_FA_Cup_final "1980 FA Cup final").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_FA_Cup_final#cite_note-FCHDWH-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_FA_Cup_final#cite_note-6)

Fulham have not played in an FA Cup final since this match. Their best run in the next 50 seasons was to the semi-finals in [2001–02](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_FA_Cup "2001–02 FA Cup") (lost 1–0 to [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.")).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_FA_Cup_final#cite_note-FCHDWH-4)

Matches were scheduled to be played at the stadium of the team named first on the date specified for each round, which was always a Saturday. If scores were level after 90 minutes had been played, a replay would take place at the stadium of the second-named team later the same week. If the replayed match was drawn further replays would be held until a winner was determined. "Dartford F.C."), [Bishop's Stortford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Stortford_F.C. "Bishop's Stortford F.C.") and [Ilford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilford_F.C. "Ilford F.C.") were given byes as the finalists from the previous season's [FA Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Trophy "FA Trophy") and [FA Amateur Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Amateur_Cup "FA Amateur Cup") respectively. During the 1974 close season the Football Association decided to abolish the distinction between amateur and professional clubs, resulting in the permanent cessation of the FA Amateur Cup. The annual finalists from the replacement competition for lower-level clubs, known as the [FA Vase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Vase "FA Vase"), would not receive byes to the first round of the FA Cup in subsequent seasons. Matches were scheduled to be played on Saturday, 23 November 1974. All games were shown in a highlights format, except the Final, which was shown live both on BBC1 and ITV. The BBC football highlights programme _[Match Of The Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match\_Of\_The\_Day "Match Of The Day")_ would show up to three games and the various ITV regional network stations would cover up to one game and show highlights from other games covered elsewhere on the ITV network. No games from rounds 1 or 2 were shown. Highlights of replays would be shown on either the BBC or ITV. **Third round**_BBC_ Orient v Derby County, Liverpool v Stoke City, Southampton v West Ham United _ITV_ Wycombe Wanderers v Middlesbrough (LWT), Manchester City v Newcastle United (Granada & Tyne-Tees), Wolverhampton Wanderers v Ipswich Town (ATV), Southend United v Queens Park Rangers (Anglia), Leeds United v Cardiff City (Yorkshire & HTV), Brighton & Hove Albion v Leatherhead (Southern), Derby County v Orient (Midweek replay All Regions). **Fourth round**_BBC_ Leatherhead v Leicester City, Plymouth Argyle v Everton, Middlesbrough v Sunderland, Arsenal v Coventry (Midweek replay), Wimbledon v Leeds United (Monday night replay) _ITV_ Ipswich Town v Liverpool (Anglia & Granada), West Ham United v Swindon Town (LWT & HTV), Coventry City v Arsenal (ATV), Leeds United v Wimbledon (Yorkshire). **Fifth round**_BBC_ Peterborough United v Middlesbrough, Arsenal v Leicester City, Mansfield Town v Carlisle United _ITV_ West Ham United v Queens Park Rangers (LWT), Everton v Fulham (Granada), Ipswich Town v Aston Villa (Anglia), Birmingham City v Walsall (ATV), Derby County v Leeds United (Midweek All regions), Leicester City v Arsenal (Midweek 2nd replay All regions). **Sixth round**_BBC_ Arsenal v West Ham United, Birmingham City v Middlesbrough _ITV_ Carlisle United v Fulham (Granada, LWT & Tyne-Tees), Ipswich Town v Leeds United (Anglia & Yorkshire), Leeds United v Ipswich Town (Midweek 2nd replay All regions) **Semi-Finals**_BBC_ Ipswich Town v West Ham United _ITV_ Birmingham City v Fulham (All regions). (Neither BBC or ITV covered the replays. The **1974–75 FA Cup** was the 94th season of the world's oldest [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[cup competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-elimination_tournament "Single-elimination tournament"), the Football Association Challenge Cup, commonly known as the [FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup"). [West Ham United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C. "West Ham United F.C.") won the competition, defeating [Second Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Second_Division "Football League Second Division") side [Fulham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulham_F.C. "Fulham F.C.") 2–0 in the [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_FA_Cup_Final "1975 FA Cup Final") at [Wembley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)"), London.

Matches were scheduled to be played at the stadium of the team named first on the date specified for each round, which was always a Saturday. If scores were level after 90 minutes had been played, a replay would take place at the stadium of the second-named team later the same week. If the replayed match was drawn further replays would be held until a winner was determined. If scores were level after 90 minutes had been played in a replay, a 30-minute period of [extra time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra_time "Extra time") would be played.

Appearing in the competition proper for the first time were Farsley Celtic, AP Leamington, Maidstone United, Leatherhead and Southwick. Of the others, Bishop Auckland, Ashford Town (Kent) and Bath City had last featured at this stage in [1966–67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966%E2%80%9367_FA_Cup "1966–67 FA Cup"), Tooting & Mitcham United had last done so in [1963-64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1963%E2%80%9364_FA_Cup "1963–64 FA Cup"), Oswestry Town and Matlcok Town had last done so in [1959–60](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959%E2%80%9360_FA_Cup "1959–60 FA Cup"), and Marine in [1947–48](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1947%E2%80%9348_FA_Cup "1947–48 FA Cup").

Gateshead United had relocated from [South Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shields "South Shields") during the summer of 1974 following the dissolution of [Gateshead AFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead_A.F.C. "Gateshead A.F.C."). Although the club had qualified for the main draw of the Cup in each of the previous six seasons under its former name, this season marked the first time a club from Gateshead would be featuring in the first round since [1965–66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965%E2%80%9366_FA_Cup "1965–66 FA Cup").

### First round proper

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1974%E2%80%9375_FA_Cup&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: First round proper")]

At this stage the 48 clubs from the [Football League Third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Third_Division "Football League Third Division") and [Fourth Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Fourth_Division "Football League Fourth Division") joined the [non-league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-League_football "Non-League football") clubs who came through the qualifying rounds. To complete this round, non-league sides [Morecambe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morecambe_F.C. "Morecambe F.C."), [Dartford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartford_F.C. "Dartford F.C."), [Bishop's Stortford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Stortford_F.C. "Bishop's Stortford F.C.") and [Ilford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilford_F.C. "Ilford F.C.") were given byes as the finalists from the previous season's [FA Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Trophy "FA Trophy") and [FA Amateur Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Amateur_Cup "FA Amateur Cup") respectively. During the 1974 close season the Football Association decided to abolish the distinction between amateur and professional clubs, resulting in the permanent cessation of the FA Amateur Cup. The annual finalists from the replacement competition for lower-level clubs, known as the [FA Vase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Vase "FA Vase"), would not receive byes to the first round of the FA Cup in subsequent seasons.

Matches were scheduled to be played on Saturday, 23 November 1974. Twelve matches were drawn, of which one required a second replay.

The right to show FA Cup games were, as with Football League matches, shared between the BBC and ITV network. All games were shown in a highlights format, except the Final, which was shown live both on BBC1 and ITV. The BBC football highlights programme _[Match Of The Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match\_Of\_The\_Day "Match Of The Day")_ would show up to three games and the various ITV regional network stations would cover up to one game and show highlights from other games covered elsewhere on the ITV network. No games from rounds 1 or 2 were shown. Highlights of replays would be shown on either the BBC or ITV.

**Third round**_BBC_ Orient v Derby County, Liverpool v Stoke City, Southampton v West Ham United _ITV_ Wycombe Wanderers v Middlesbrough (LWT), Manchester City v Newcastle United (Granada & Tyne-Tees), Wolverhampton Wanderers v Ipswich Town (ATV), Southend United v Queens Park Rangers (Anglia), Leeds United v Cardiff City (Yorkshire & HTV), Brighton & Hove Albion v Leatherhead (Southern), Derby County v Orient (Midweek replay All Regions).

**Fourth round**_BBC_ Leatherhead v Leicester City, Plymouth Argyle v Everton, Middlesbrough v Sunderland, Arsenal v Coventry (Midweek replay), Wimbledon v Leeds United (Monday night replay) _ITV_ Ipswich Town v Liverpool (Anglia & Granada), West Ham United v Swindon Town (LWT & HTV), Coventry City v Arsenal (ATV), Leeds United v Wimbledon (Yorkshire).

**Fifth round**_BBC_ Peterborough United v Middlesbrough, Arsenal v Leicester City, Mansfield Town v Carlisle United _ITV_ West Ham United v Queens Park Rangers (LWT), Everton v Fulham (Granada), Ipswich Town v Aston Villa (Anglia), Birmingham City v Walsall (ATV), Derby County v Leeds United (Midweek All regions), Leicester City v Arsenal (Midweek 2nd replay All regions).

**Sixth round**_BBC_ Arsenal v West Ham United, Birmingham City v Middlesbrough _ITV_ Carlisle United v Fulham (Granada, LWT & Tyne-Tees), Ipswich Town v Leeds United (Anglia & Yorkshire), Leeds United v Ipswich Town (Midweek 2nd replay All regions)

**Semi-Finals**_BBC_ Ipswich Town v West Ham United _ITV_ Birmingham City v Fulham (All regions). (Neither BBC or ITV covered the replays. The goals were only shown as clips for TV news reports.)

**Final** Fulham v West Ham United shown live on both BBC and ITV.

**West Ham United Football Club** is a professional [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club based in [Stratford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratford,_London "Stratford, London"), [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London "East London"), England. The club currently competes in the [EFL Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EFL_Championship "EFL Championship") in the [2026–27 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026%E2%80%9327_EFL_Championship "2026–27 EFL Championship") following relegation from the [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League"). The club plays at the [London Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Stadium "London Stadium"), having moved from their former home, the [Boleyn Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground"), in 2016.

West Ham United was founded in 1895 as [Thames Ironworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Ironworks_F.C. "Thames Ironworks F.C.") and reformed in 1900 as West Ham United. It moved to the Boleyn Ground, which remained its home ground for more than a century, in 1904. The team initially competed in the [Southern League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Football_League "Southern Football League") and [Western League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Football_League "Western Football League") before joining the [Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Football_League "English Football League") in 1919. It was promoted to the top flight in 1923, when it was also losing finalist in the first [FA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_FA_Cup_final "1923 FA Cup final") held at [Wembley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)"). In 1940, the club won the inaugural [Football League War Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_War_Cup "Football League War Cup").

West Ham United has won five major honours in its history. Domestically, it has been winner of the [FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup") three times (1964, 1975 and 1980) and runner-up twice (1923 and 2006). In European competitions, the club has reached three major European finals winning the [European Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup "UEFA Cup Winners' Cup") in [1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964%E2%80%9365_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup "1964–65 European Cup Winners' Cup"), finishing runner-up in the same competitions in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup "1975–76 European Cup Winners' Cup"), and winning the second edition of the [Conference League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Conference_League "UEFA Conference League") in [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_UEFA_Europa_Conference_League "2022–23 UEFA Europa Conference League"). The club has also won one minor European trophy by winning the [Intertoto Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Intertoto_Cup "UEFA Intertoto Cup") in 1999. West Ham United is one of eight clubs never to have fallen below the second tier of English football, spending 68 of 100 league seasons in the top flight, up to and including the [2025–26 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Premier_League "2025–26 Premier League"). The club's highest league position to date came in [1985–86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985%E2%80%9386_Football_League "1985–86 Football League"), when it achieved third place in the then [First Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_First_Division "Football League First Division").

Three West Ham players were members of the [1966 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_FIFA_World_Cup "1966 FIFA World Cup") finals-winning [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") team: captain [Bobby Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Moore "Bobby Moore") and goalscorers [Geoff Hurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Hurst "Geoff Hurst") and [Martin Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Peters "Martin Peters"). The club has a [long-standing rivalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millwall_F.C.%E2%80%93West_Ham_United_F.C._rivalry "Millwall F.C.–West Ham United F.C. rivalry") with [Millwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millwall_F.C. "Millwall F.C."), and the fixture has gained notoriety for frequent incidents of [football hooliganism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_hooliganism "Football hooliganism"). West Ham adopted their [claret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_red "Wine red"), [sky blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_blue "Sky blue") and white colour scheme in the early 1900s, with the most common iteration of a claret shirt and sky blue sleeves first emerging in 1904.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-4)

## History

Main article: [History of West Ham United F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Ham_United_F.C. "History of West Ham United F.C.")

### Origins

Main article: [Thames Ironworks F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Ironworks_F.C. "Thames Ironworks F.C.")

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/ThamesIronworksFC.gif/250px-ThamesIronworksFC.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ThamesIronworksFC.gif)

Earliest club shot, during its founding year as Thames Ironworks in 1895

The earliest generally accepted incarnation of West Ham United was founded in 1895 as [Thames Ironworks F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Ironworks_F.C. "Thames Ironworks F.C."), the [works team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Works_team "Works team") of the largest and last surviving shipbuilder on the Thames, [Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Ironworks_and_Shipbuilding_Company "Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company"), by foreman and local league referee [Dave Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Taylor_(Thames_Ironworks_F.C._founder) "Dave Taylor (Thames Ironworks F.C. founder)") and owner [Arnold Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Hills "Arnold Hills")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Spartacus1-5) and was announced in the _Thames Ironworks Gazette_ of June 1895. Thames Ironworks was based in [Leamouth Wharf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leamouth "Leamouth") in [Blackwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackwall,_London "Blackwall, London") and [Canning Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canning_Town "Canning Town") on both banks of the [River Lea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Lea "River Lea"), where the Lea meets the [Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames"). Thames Ironworks built many ships and other structures, the most famous being [HMS _Warrior_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Warrior_(1860) "HMS Warrior (1860)"). The last ship built there was the [dreadnought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreadnought "Dreadnought")[HMS _Thunderer_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Thunderer_(1911) "HMS Thunderer (1911)") in 1912 and the yard shut soon after.

The repair yard of the [Castle Shipping Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union-Castle_Line "Union-Castle Line") was a very near neighbour and their work team, initially known as the [Castle Swifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Castle_Swifts_F.C. "Old Castle Swifts F.C."), would informally merge with the Thames Ironworks own team. The team played on a strictly amateur basis for 1895 at least, with a team featuring a number of works employees. Thomas Freeman was a ships fireman and Walter Parks, a clerk. [Johnny Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Stewart_(footballer,_born_1872) "Johnny Stewart (footballer, born 1872)"), [Walter Tranter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Tranter "Walter Tranter") and [James Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Lindsay_(footballer,_born_1870) "Jamie Lindsay (footballer, born 1870)") were all boilermakers. Other employees included William Chapman, [George Sage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Sage_(footballer) "George Sage (footballer)") and Fred Chamberlain, as well as apprentice riveter [Charlie Dove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Dove "Charlie Dove"), who was to have a great influence on the club's future at a later date.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-6)

Thames Ironworks won the [West Ham Charity Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_Charity_Cup "West Ham Charity Cup"), contested by clubs in the [West Ham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham "West Ham") locality, in 1895, then won the [London League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_League_(football) "London League (football)") in 1897. They turned professional in 1898 upon entering the [Southern League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Football_League "Southern Football League") Second Division, and were promoted to the First Division at the first attempt. The following year they came second from bottom, but had established themselves as a fully-fledged competitive team. They comfortably fended off the challenge of local rivals [Fulham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulham_F.C. "Fulham F.C.") in a relegation play-off, 5–1 in late April 1900 and retained their First Division status.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Stats1-7)

Following growing disputes over the running and financing of the club, in June 1900 Thames Ironworks F.C. was disbanded, then almost immediately relaunched as West Ham United F.C. – reflecting the [West Ham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham "West Ham"), London district where they played – on 5 July 1900 with [Syd King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_King "Syd King") as their manager and future manager [Charlie Paynter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Paynter "Charlie Paynter") as his assistant. Because of the original "works team" roots and links (still represented upon the club badge), they are still known as "the Irons" or "the Hammers" amongst fans and the media.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-EastLon-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-9)

### Birth of West Ham United (1901–1961)

West Ham United joined the Western League for the 1901 season[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Stats2-10) while also continuing to play in the Southern Division 1. In 1907, West Ham were crowned the Western League Division 1B Champions, and then defeated 1A champions Fulham 1–0 to become the Western League Overall Champions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Stats2-10) The reborn club continued to play their games at the [Memorial Grounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Grounds "Memorial Grounds") in [Plaistow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaistow,_Newham "Plaistow, Newham") (funded by Arnold Hills) but moved to a [pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football_pitch "Association football pitch") in the Upton Park area in the guise of the [Boleyn Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground") stadium in 1904. West Ham's first game in their new home was against fierce [rivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millwall_F.C.%E2%80%93West_Ham_United_F.C._rivalry "Millwall F.C.–West Ham United F.C. rivalry")[Millwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millwall_F.C. "Millwall F.C.") (themselves an Ironworks team, albeit for a rival company) drawing a crowd of 10,000 and with West Ham running out 3–0 winners,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-11) and as the _[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_ wrote on 2 September 1904, "Favoured by the weather turning fine after heavy rains of the morning, West Ham United began their season most auspiciously yesterday evening; when they beat Millwall by 3 goals to 0 on their new enclosure at Upton Park."

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Whitehorsefinal.jpg/250px-Whitehorsefinal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whitehorsefinal.jpg)

_Billie_ the White Horse, saviour of the 1923 [FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup") final

In 1919, still under King's leadership, West Ham gained entrance to the [Football League Second Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Second_Division "Football League Second Division"), their first game being a 1–1 draw with [Lincoln City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_City_F.C. "Lincoln City F.C."), and were promoted to the [First Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_First_Division "Football League First Division") in 1923, also making it to the first ever [FA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup_final "FA Cup final") to be held at the old [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)"). Their opponents were [Bolton Wanderers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolton_Wanderers_F.C. "Bolton Wanderers F.C."). This was also known as the "[White Horse final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Horse_final "White Horse final")", where nearly 300,000 people (according to Police estimates)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Belton_1983_128-12) came to see the match. Overcrowding led to the crowd spilling out on to the pitch, which had to be cleared prior to kick-off by "Billie", a giant white horse (actually grey) being ridden by PC [George Scorey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Scorey "George Scorey"). The cup final match itself ended 2–0 to Bolton. The team enjoyed mixed success in the First Division but retained their status for ten years and reached the FA Cup semi-final in 1933.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-1933semi-13)

In 1932, the club was relegated to the Second Division[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-14) and long-term custodian [Syd King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_King "Syd King") was sacked after serving the club in the role of manager for 32 years, and as a player from 1899 to 1903. Following relegation, King had mental health problems. He appeared drunk at a board meeting and killed himself soon after.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-15) He was replaced with his assistant manager [Charlie Paynter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Paynter "Charlie Paynter"), who himself had been with West Ham in a number of roles since 1897 and who went on to serve the team in this role until 1950 for a total of 480 games. At the start of the [1939–1940](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939%E2%80%9340_Football_League#Second_Division "1939–40 Football League") season, the club has assembled a group of players that Charlie Paynter believed was the most talented he'd managed. This included local men brought through the youth team such as [Len Goulden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Len_Goulden "Len Goulden"), an England regular, and successful signings from the English and Scottish Leagues. There was hope for promotion and a successful new era until war broke out three matches into the season and league football was suspended for six years.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Korr_1986_148-16)

Although league competition was suspended, the [War Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_War_Cup "Football League War Cup") was played in place of the FA Cup for the duration of hostilities. In June 1940 the club won its first major trophy, winning the War Cup by beating first division [Blackburn Rovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackburn_Rovers_F.C. "Blackburn Rovers F.C.") 1–0 at Wembley Stadium.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Korr_1986_148-16) The club spent most of the next thirty years in the second division, first under Paynter and then later under the leadership of former player [Ted Fenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Fenton "Ted Fenton"). Fenton succeeded in getting the club promoted back to the top level of English football in 1958. With the considerable input of player [Malcolm Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Allison "Malcolm Allison"), Fenton helped develop both the initial batch of future West Ham stars and West Ham's approach to the game.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-20)

### Glory years (1961–1986)

[Ron Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Greenwood "Ron Greenwood") was appointed as Fenton's successor in 1961 and soon led the club to two major trophies, winning the [1964 FA Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_FA_Cup_Final "1964 FA Cup Final"). The team was led by the young [Bobby Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Moore "Bobby Moore"). West Ham also won the [European Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final "1965 UEFA Cup Winners' Cup Final") the following year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-rg-22) During the [1966 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_FIFA_World_Cup "1966 FIFA World Cup"), key members of the tournament winners [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") were West Ham players, including the captain, [Bobby Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Moore "Bobby Moore"); [Martin Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Peters "Martin Peters") (who scored in the final); and [Geoff Hurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Hurst "Geoff Hurst"), who scored the first [hat-trick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hat-trick "Hat-trick") in a [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup") final.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-rg-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-23) All three players had come through the youth team at West Ham.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-24)

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Champions_statue.jpg/250px-Champions_statue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Champions_statue.jpg)

Champions statue on Barking Road

There is a "Champions" statue in [Barking Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barking_Road "Barking Road"), opposite The [Boleyn Tavern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Tavern "Boleyn Tavern"), commemorating West Ham's "three sons" who helped win the 1966 World Cup: Bobby Moore, Geoff Hurst and Martin Peters. Also included on the statue is [Everton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everton_F.C. "Everton F.C.")'s [Ray Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Wilson_(English_footballer) "Ray Wilson (English footballer)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-25) After a difficult start to the 1974–75 season, Greenwood moved himself "upstairs" to become general manager and, without informing the board, appointed his assistant [John Lyall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lyall "John Lyall") as team manager.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-26) The result was instant success – the team scored 20 goals in their first four games and won the FA Cup, becoming the last team to win the FA Cup with an all-English side when they beat Fulham 2–0 in the 1975 final.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-27) The Fulham team included two former England [captains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(association_football) "Captain (association football)"), [Alan Mullery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Mullery "Alan Mullery") and West Ham legend Bobby Moore.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-28) Lyall then guided West Ham to another [European Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final "1976 UEFA Cup Winners' Cup Final") final in 1976, though the team lost the match 4–2 to Belgian side [Anderlecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSC_Anderlecht "RSC Anderlecht").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-29) Greenwood's tenure as general manager lasted less than three years, as he was appointed to manage England in the wake of [Don Revie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Revie "Don Revie")'s resignation in 1977.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-exitrevie-30)

In 1978, West Ham were again relegated to the Second Division, but Lyall was retained as manager and led the team to victory in the [1980 FA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_FA_Cup_final "1980 FA Cup final") with a 1–0 win against [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_F.C. "Arsenal F.C."), the most recent time a team from outside the top flight has won the FA Cup.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-31) They reached the final by defeating Everton in the semi-final.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-32) West Ham were promoted to the First Division in 1981, and finished in the top ten of the First Division for the next three seasons before achieving their highest-ever league finish of third in 1985–86; a group of players which came to be known as [The Boys of 86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Boys_of_86 "The Boys of 86").

### Ups and downs (1986–2005)

However, the _Hammers_ suffered relegation again in 1989, which resulted in Lyall's sacking.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-33) He was awarded an _ex gratia_ payment of [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_sterling "Pound sterling")100,000 (equivalent to £265,000 in 2025) but left the club in what Lyall described as "upsetting" circumstances, meriting only 73 words in a terse acknowledgement of his service in the club programme. Lyall left West Ham after 34 years' service.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-34)

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/WestHamUtdFC_League_Performance.svg/250px-WestHamUtdFC_League_Performance.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WestHamUtdFC_League_Performance.svg)

Yearly performance of West Ham since joining the Football League

After Lyall, [Lou Macari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Macari "Lou Macari") briefly led the team, though he resigned after less than a single season in order to clear his name of allegations of illegal betting while manager of [Swindon Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swindon_Town_F.C. "Swindon Town F.C.").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-35) He was replaced by former player [Billy Bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Bonds "Billy Bonds").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-essential-36) In Bonds' first full season, [1990–91](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990%E2%80%9391_in_English_football "1990–91 in English football"), West Ham again secured promotion to the First Division. Now back in the top flight, Bonds saw West Ham through one of their most controversial seasons. With the club planning to introduce a [bond scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debenture_(sport) "Debenture (sport)"), there was crowd unrest. West Ham finished last and were relegated back to the Second Division after only one season.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Protest1-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-BrownOut-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-TEHOWHU197-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Storrie-40) However, they rebounded strongly in 1992–93. With [Trevor Morley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Morley "Trevor Morley") and [Clive Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Allen "Clive Allen") scoring 40 goals, they guaranteed themselves second place on the last day of the season with a 2–0 home win against [Cambridge United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_United_F.C. "Cambridge United F.C."), and with it promotion to the [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993%E2%80%9394_Premier_League "1993–94 Premier League").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-42)

[![Image 41](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/WestHamUnitedBus2005.JPG/250px-WestHamUnitedBus2005.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WestHamUnitedBus2005.JPG)

West Ham players on open-top bus near [Upton Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground") celebrate winning the 2005 play-off final in Cardiff. From L-R [Shaun Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun_Newton "Shaun Newton") (crouching), Back row, [Matthew Etherington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Etherington "Matthew Etherington"), [Jimmy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Walker_(footballer_born_1973) "James Walker (footballer born 1973)"), [Teddy Sheringham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Sheringham "Teddy Sheringham"), [Marlon Harewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlon_Harewood "Marlon Harewood"), Front row [Don Hutchison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Hutchison "Don Hutchison"), [Carl Fletcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Fletcher_(Welsh_footballer) "Carl Fletcher (Welsh footballer)"), [Elliott Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_Ward "Elliott Ward") and [Mark Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Noble "Mark Noble") (with flag).

With the team in the Premier League, there was a need to rebuild the team. [Oxford United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_United_F.C. "Oxford United F.C.") player [Joey Beauchamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Beauchamp "Joey Beauchamp") was recruited for a fee of £1.2 million (equivalent to £2.6 million in 2025). Shortly after arriving at the club, however, he became unhappy, citing homesickness from his native Oxford as the reason. Bonds in particular found this attitude hard to understand compared to his own committed, never-say-die approach; providing for Bonds' further evidence of the decay in the modern game and modern player.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-43) Fifty-eight days later, Beauchamp was signed by Swindon Town for a club-record combined fee of £800,000 (equivalent to £1.7 million in 2025), which included defender [Adrian Whitbread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Whitbread "Adrian Whitbread") going in the opposite direction. Whitbread was valued at £750,000 (equivalent to £1.5 million in 2025) in the deal.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-44)

Assistant manager [Harry Redknapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Redknapp "Harry Redknapp") was also now taking a bigger role in the transfer of players, with the club's approval. With rumours of his old club [AFC Bournemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Bournemouth "AFC Bournemouth") being prepared to offer him a position,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-45) the West Ham board and their managing director, [Peter Storrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Storrie "Peter Storrie"), made a controversial move. The board were anxious not to lose Redknapp's services and offered Bonds a place away from the day-to-day affairs of the club on the West Ham board. This would have allowed them to appoint Redknapp as manager. Bonds refused the post offered and walked away from the club.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-BMTHOTB146-46) His accusations of deceit and manipulation by the board and by Redknapp have continued to cause ill-feeling.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-BMTHOTB146-46) Peter Storrie claimed that they had handled the situation correctly, saying, "If Harry had gone to Bournemouth, there was a good chance Bill would have resigned anyway, so we were in a no-win situation. We're sad that Bill is going, and it's a big blow but it's time to move on and we have appointed a great manager."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-47) Redknapp became manager on 10 August 1994.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-14m-48)

Redknapp's seven years as manager was notable for the turnover of players during his tenure and for the level of attractive football and success which had not been seen since the managership of John Lyall. Over 134 players passed through the club while he was manager, producing a net transfer fee deficit of £16 million, despite the £18 million sale (equivalent to £34.2 million in 2025) of [Rio Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Ferdinand "Rio Ferdinand") to [Leeds United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_United_F.C. "Leeds United F.C.") in 2000.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-fees-49) Some were notably successful, such as the signings of [Stuart Pearce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Pearce "Stuart Pearce"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50)[Trevor Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Sinclair "Trevor Sinclair"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50)[Paolo Di Canio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Di_Canio "Paolo Di Canio"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50)[John Hartson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hartson "John Hartson"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50)[Eyal Berkovic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyal_Berkovic "Eyal Berkovic")[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50) and [Ian Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Wright "Ian Wright").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-wrightwrightwright-51) Meanwhile, some were expensive, international players who failed at West Ham, such as [Florin Raducioiu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florin_Raducioiu "Florin Raducioiu");[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50)[Davor Šuker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davor_%C5%A0uker "Davor Šuker"), who earned as much in wages as the revenue gained from one entire stand and yet made only eight appearances;[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-fees-49)[Christian Bassila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Bassila "Christian Bassila"), who cost £720,000 (equivalent to £1.4 million in 2025) and played only 86 minutes of football;[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-fees-49)[Titi Camara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titi_Camara "Titi Camara"); [Gary Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Charles "Gary Charles"), whose wages amounted to £4.4 million (equivalent to £8.2 million in 2025) but made only three starts for the club;[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-fees-49)[Rigobert Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigobert_Song "Rigobert Song"); [Paulo Futre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Futre "Paulo Futre");[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50) and [Marco Boogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Boogers "Marco Boogers"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50) a player often quoted as one of the biggest failures in the Premier League.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Boogers-52) His first season in charge saw West Ham fighting the threat of relegation until the last few weeks,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-53) while his third season would also see another relegation battle. Always willing to enter the transfer market, Redknapp bought in the winter transfer window John Hartson and [Paul Kitson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kitson "Paul Kitson"), who added the impetus needed at the season's end.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-54)

In 1999, West Ham finished fifth, their highest position in the top flight since 1986.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50) They also won the [Intertoto Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertoto_Cup "Intertoto Cup") beating French club [Metz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Metz "FC Metz") to qualify for the [1999–2000 UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_UEFA_Cup "1999–2000 UEFA Cup").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-hr-50)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-intertotocupwin-55) Things began to falter for Redknapp with the sale of Ferdinand to Leeds in November 2000. Redknapp used the transfer money poorly with purchases such as [Ragnvald Soma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnvald_Soma "Ragnvald Soma"), who cost £800,000 (equivalent to £1.5 million in 2025) and played only seven league games, Camara, and Song. Redknapp felt he needed more funds with which to deal in the transfer market.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-cash-56) Chairman [Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Brown_(football_chairman) "Terry Brown (football chairman)") lost patience with Redknapp due to his demands for further transfer funds. In June 2001, called to a meeting with Brown expecting to discuss contracts, he was fired.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-cash-56) His assistant [Frank Lampard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lampard_Sr. "Frank Lampard Sr.") left too, making the sale of his son, [Frank Lampard Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lampard "Frank Lampard"), inevitable;[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-cash-56) in the summer of 2001, he joined [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") for £11 million (equivalent to £20.7 million in 2025).[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-57)

With several names, such as former player [Alan Curbishley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Curbishley "Alan Curbishley"), now linked with the job, Chairman Brown recruited from within the club,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-cash-56) appointing reserve team coach [Glenn Roeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Roeder "Glenn Roeder") as manager on 9 May 2001.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-14m-48) He had already failed in management with [Gillingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillingham_F.C. "Gillingham F.C."), where he lost 22 of the 35 games he managed, and [Watford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watford_F.C. "Watford F.C.").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-ncfc-58) His first big signings were the return of [Don Hutchison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Hutchison "Don Hutchison") for £5 million (equivalent to £9.4 million in 2025)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-59) and Czech centre back [Tomáš Řepka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom%C3%A1%C5%A1_%C5%98epka "Tomáš Řepka").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-60) Finishing seventh in his first season[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-61) Roeder, in his office at [Upton Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground"), suffered a blocked blood vessel in his brain.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-ncfc-58)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-sirtrev-62) As Roeder needed medical help and recuperation, former stalwart [Trevor Brooking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Brooking "Trevor Brooking") stood in as caretaker manager.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-sirtrev-62) Despite not losing another game, the Hammers were relegated on the last day of the season at [Birmingham City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_F.C. "Birmingham City F.C."), with a record high for a relegated club of 42 points from a 38-game season. Ten seasons of top-tier football were over.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-63) Many top players, including [Joe Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Cole "Joe Cole"), Di Canio and Kanouté, all left the club. The next season, now in the second tier, Roeder resumed his stint as manager. Results were still poor, however, and after an away defeat to [Rotherham United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotherham_United_F.C. "Rotherham United F.C."), he was sacked on 24 August 2003.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-ncfc-58) Brooking again took over as caretaker.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-64) He lost only one game, a 2–0 away defeat to [Gillingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillingham_F.C. "Gillingham F.C."),[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-65) and is known as "the best manager West Ham never had".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-66)

Former [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_F.C. "Crystal Palace F.C.") player and manager of [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_F.C. "Reading F.C."), [Alan Pardew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Pardew "Alan Pardew") was lined up to be the next bench boss. Reading and their chairman, [John Madejski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Madejski "John Madejski"), however, were reluctant to let him leave.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-67) After serving a period of notice and gardening leave, and with West Ham paying Reading £380,000 (equivalent to £695,000 in 2025) in compensation, he was appointed manager on 18 October 2003, their tenth manager.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-68) Pardew set out to rebuild the side bringing in [Nigel Reo-Coker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Reo-Coker "Nigel Reo-Coker"),[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-pards-69)[Marlon Harewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlon_Harewood "Marlon Harewood")[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-70) and [Brian Deane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Deane "Brian Deane").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-71) In his first season in charge, they made the playoff final only to lose to Crystal Palace.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-72) His signings of [Bobby Zamora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Zamora "Bobby Zamora"), [Matthew Etherington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Etherington "Matthew Etherington") and veterans [Chris Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Powell "Chris Powell") and [Teddy Sheringham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Sheringham "Teddy Sheringham") saw West Ham finishing sixth and subsequently beat [Preston North End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_North_End_F.C. "Preston North End F.C.") 1–0 thanks to a Zamora goal in the [2005 playoff final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Football_League_Championship_play-off_Final "2005 Football League Championship play-off Final"), securing a return to the Premier League.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-73) After ensuring promotion, Pardew said, "It's a team effort. We defended well and we're back where we belong."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-74)

### Final years at the Boleyn (2005–2016)

On their return to the top division, West Ham finished in ninth place,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-Final_2005/2006_English_Premier_Table-75) The highlight of the [2005–06 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_West_Ham_United_F.C._season "2005–06 West Ham United F.C. season"), however, was reaching the [FA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FA_Cup_final "2006 FA Cup final") and taking favourites [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") to a [penalty shootout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shootout_(association_football) "Penalty shootout (association football)") after a 3–3 draw. West Ham lost the shootout, but nonetheless gained entry to the following season's [UEFA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_UEFA_Cup "2006–07 UEFA Cup") as Liverpool had already qualified for the [Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_UEFA_Champions_League "2006–07 UEFA Champions League"). In August 2006, West Ham completed a major coup on the last day of the transfer window after completing the signings of [Carlos Tevez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Tevez "Carlos Tevez") and [Javier Mascherano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javier_Mascherano "Javier Mascherano").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-West_Ham_sign_Tevez_&_Mascherano-76) The club was eventually bought by an [Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland") consortium, led by [Eggert Magnússon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggert_Magn%C3%BAsson "Eggert Magnússon"), in November 2006.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-77) Manager Alan Pardew was sacked after poor form during the season[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-78) and was replaced by former [Charlton Athletic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlton_Athletic_F.C. "Charlton Athletic F.C.") manager [Alan Curbishley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Curbishley "Alan Curbishley").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-curb-79)

The signings of Mascherano and Tevez were investigated by the Premier League, who were concerned that details of the transfers had been omitted from official records. The club was found guilty and fined £5.5 million in April 2007.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-80) However, West Ham avoided a points deduction which ultimately became critical in their avoidance of relegation at the end of the [2006–07 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_Premier_League "2006–07 Premier League"). Following on from this event, [Wigan Athletic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigan_Athletic_F.C. "Wigan Athletic F.C.") chairman [Dave Whelan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Whelan "Dave Whelan"), supported by other sides facing possible relegation, including Fulham and [Sheffield United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheffield_United_F.C. "Sheffield United F.C."), threatened legal action.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-81) West Ham escaped relegation by winning seven of their last nine games, including a 1–0 win over Arsenal, and on the last day of the season defeated newly crowned League Champions [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") 1–0 with a goal by Tevez to finish 15th.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-82)

In the [2007–08 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_in_English_football "2007–08 in English football"), West Ham remained reasonably consistently in the top half of the league table, with [Freddie Ljungberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Ljungberg "Freddie Ljungberg") in the team, despite a slew of injuries; new signing [Craig Bellamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Bellamy "Craig Bellamy") missed most of the campaign, while [Kieron Dyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kieron_Dyer "Kieron Dyer") was out from August 2007.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-84) The last game of the season, at the [Boleyn Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground"), saw West Ham draw 2–2 against [Aston Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_F.C. "Aston Villa F.C."), ensuring a tenth-place finish three points ahead of rivals [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C."). It was a five-place improvement on the previous season, and most importantly West Ham were never under any realistic threat of relegation. After a row with the board over the sale of defenders [Anton Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Ferdinand "Anton Ferdinand") and [George McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_McCartney_(footballer) "George McCartney (footballer)") to [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland_A.F.C. "Sunderland A.F.C."), manager Alan Curbishley resigned on 3 September 2008.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-85) His successor was former Chelsea striker [Gianfranco Zola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianfranco_Zola "Gianfranco Zola"), who took over on 11 September 2008 to become the club's first non-British manager.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-zola1-86) In the [2008–09 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008%E2%80%9309_in_English_football "2008–09 in English football"), West Ham finished ninth, a single place improvement.

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/2012_Football_League_Championship_play-off_Final_Nolan_lifts_the_cup.jpg/500px-2012_Football_League_Championship_play-off_Final_Nolan_lifts_the_cup.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012_Football_League_Championship_play-off_Final_Nolan_lifts_the_cup.jpg)

[Kevin Nolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Nolan "Kevin Nolan") lifts the trophy after the [2012 Football League Championship play-off final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Football_League_Championship_play-off_final "2012 Football League Championship play-off final").

In the [2009–10 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009%E2%80%9310_in_English_football "2009–10 in English football"), West Ham started strongly with a 2–0 win over newly promoted [Wolverhampton Wanderers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverhampton_Wanderers_F.C. "Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C."), with goals from [Mark Noble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Noble "Mark Noble") and newly appointed captain [Matthew Upson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Upson "Matthew Upson").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-87) A [League Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Cup "Football League Cup")[match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Upton_Park_riot "2009 Upton Park riot") against old rivals [Millwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millwall_F.C. "Millwall F.C.") brought about violent riots outside the ground as well as [pitch invasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_invasion "Pitch invasion") and crowd trouble inside [Upton Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-88) In August 2009, the financial concerns of Icelandic owners parent companies left the current owners unable to provide any funds until a new owner was found. The club's shirt sponsor [SBOBET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBOBET "SBOBET") provided the club with help to purchase a much needed striker, the Italian [Alessandro Diamanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Diamanti "Alessandro Diamanti").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-89)

West Ham had a poor season which involved a prolonged battle against relegation.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-zola2010-90) They finally secured their survival with two games remaining by defeating Wigan 3–2.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-91) The club managed to take 35 points from 38 games, seven fewer than the total they had when relegated seven years prior.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-zola2010-90) On 11 May 2010, two days after the end of the 2009–10 season, West Ham announced the termination of Zola's contract with immediate effect.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-92) On 3 June 2010, [Avram Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avram_Grant "Avram Grant") signed a four-year deal to become the next manager of West Ham subject to a [work permit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_permit_(United_Kingdom) "Work permit (United Kingdom)").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-93) West Ham's form continued to be poor with the team seldom outside the relegation zone,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-94) placing Grant's future as manager under serious doubt.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-95) A 4–0 [Football League Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Cup "Football League Cup") quarter-final win over Manchester United was an otherwise bright spot in a disappointing season.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-96) West Ham's form in the Premier League did not affect their form in the two domestic cups. The Hammers reached the semi-final of the League Cup before being eliminated by eventual winners [Birmingham City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_F.C. "Birmingham City F.C.") as well as the quarter-final of the FA Cup before a 2–1 defeat at eventual runners-up [Stoke City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_City_F.C. "Stoke City F.C.").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-98)

On 15 May 2011, West Ham's relegation to [the Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Football_League_Championship "2011–12 Football League Championship") was confirmed after a comeback from Wigan at the [DW Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DW_Stadium "DW Stadium"). With West Ham leading 2–0 at half-time through two [Demba Ba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demba_Ba "Demba Ba") goals, Wigan battled back to win 3–2 thanks to an added-time strike from [Charles N'Zogbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_N'Zogbia "Charles N'Zogbia"). Following the loss, West Ham announced the [sacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dismissal_(employment) "Dismissal (employment)") of manager Avram Grant just one season into his tenure.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-99) On 1 June 2011, [Sam Allardyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Allardyce "Sam Allardyce") was appointed as manager as Grant's replacement.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-100) The club finished third in the [2011–12 Football League Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Football_League_Championship "2011–12 Football League Championship") with 86 points and took part in the play-offs. They beat [Cardiff City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_City_F.C. "Cardiff City F.C.") in the play-off semi-final 5–0 on aggregate to reach the final against [Blackpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpool_F.C "Blackpool F.C") at [Wembley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium "Wembley Stadium") on 19 May 2012. [Carlton Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlton_Cole "Carlton Cole") opened the scoring, and although Blackpool equalised early in the second half, [Ricardo Vaz Tê](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Vaz_T%C3%AA "Ricardo Vaz Tê") scored the winner for West Ham in the 87th minute.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-101)

West Ham, on their return to the Premier League, signed former players [James Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Collins_(footballer,_born_1983) "James Collins (footballer, born 1983)") and [George McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_McCartney_(footballer) "George McCartney (footballer)") on permanent deals, as well as record signing [Matt Jarvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Jarvis "Matt Jarvis") and [Andy Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Carroll "Andy Carroll") on loan.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-105) They won their first game of the season, on 18 August 2012, 1–0 against [Aston Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_F.C. "Aston Villa F.C.") thanks to a [Kevin Nolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Nolan "Kevin Nolan") goal.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-106) The highlight of the first half of the season was a 3–1 home win against reigning [European champions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_UEFA_Champions_League_Final "2012 UEFA Champions League Final")[Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_F.C. "Chelsea F.C.") on 1 December 2012 which saw them in eighth position[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-107) and 12th at the end of the year.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-108) On 22 March 2013, West Ham secured a 99-year lease deal on the [Olympic Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Stadium "London Stadium"), with it planned to be used as their home ground from the 2016–17 season.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-109) Tenth place was secured at the end of the season with nine home wins and only three away from home. "Manchester City F.C.").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-2014_league_cup_semi-112) A feature of the season were the criticisms of manager Sam Allardyce by supporters relating to his perceived negative playing tactics.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-samout1-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-samout2-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-samout3-115) West Ham finished 12th in the [2014–15 Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Premier_League "2014–15 Premier League"), one place higher than the previous season. ### Move to London Stadium and European success (2016–2023)

Following Manchester United's win in the [2016 FA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_FA_Cup_final "2016 FA Cup final"), West Ham took their Europa League place and qualified for the third qualifying round of the [2016–17 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_UEFA_Europa_League "2016–17 UEFA Europa League").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-europe201617-121) At the end of the [first season at the London Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Premier_League "2016–17 Premier League"), the team finished 11th, along with having to deal with the departure of star man [Dimitri Payet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitri_Payet "Dimitri Payet").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-122) However, the team suffered a poor start to the following season, taking only two wins in their opening 11 games. Following a 4–1 defeat to Liverpool at home and with the team threatened by relegation, Bilić was sacked on 6 November 2017. He was replaced by former Sunderland boss [David Moyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Moyes "David Moyes") on a contract until the end of the season. The team battled inconsistent form for the rest of the season but managed to avoid relegation and finish 13th. Moyes was not offered a new contract and left the club on the expiration of it on 16 May 2018.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-123)

On 22 May 2018, the club appointed former [Manchester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_City_F.C. "Manchester City F.C.") boss [Manuel Pellegrini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Pellegrini "Manuel Pellegrini") as the new manager on a three-year contract.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-WestHamIn-124) In his first season in charge, the Hammers finished 10th, once again suffering from inconsistent form. However, after a poor first half to the following season, Pellegrini was sacked in December 2019 with the team only one point above the relegation zone. His last game in charge was a 2–1 home loss to Leicester City.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-125) He was replaced by David Moyes, who returned for a second spell in charge a day later.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-126)

On 22 July 2020, the club secured their Premier League status for another season, following a 1–1 draw away to Manchester United.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-127) Ahead of the [2020–21 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_West_Ham_United_F.C._season "2020–21 West Ham United F.C. season"), West Ham's ownership attracted criticism, including from club captain Mark Noble who publicly criticized the sale of academy graduate [Grady Diangana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grady_Diangana "Grady Diangana").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-128) Despite losing the opening two games of the season, West Ham's form improved and by the end of November, the club sat in fifth place.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-129) The club would not drop out of a European spot for the rest of the season and went on to qualify for the [2021–22 UEFA Europa League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_UEFA_Europa_League "2021–22 UEFA Europa League") group stages after finishing in 6th.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-130) Moyes signed a new three-year contract on 12 June 2021.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-131)

West Ham won their first three games of the year 2022, temporarily elevating the club to fourth place in the Premier League.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-2122Stats-132) The team beat [Sevilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevilla_FC "Sevilla FC") 2–1 on aggregate to reach a first European quarter-final in 41 years,[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-133) followed by a 4–1 aggregate win over [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_Lyonnais "Olympique Lyonnais") for a first such semi-final since 1976.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-134) Playing the same opposition they met in their 1976 [European Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup "UEFA Cup Winners' Cup") semi-final, [Eintracht Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eintracht_Frankfurt "Eintracht Frankfurt"), West Ham were knocked out of the Europa League, following a 3–1 aggregate loss to the German side.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-135) At the end of the [2021–22 Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Premier_League "2021–22 Premier League") season, West Ham confirmed a second successive season of European football, qualifying for the [UEFA Europa Conference League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Europa_Conference_League "UEFA Europa Conference League") after finishing seventh. The club finished 14th in the Premier League, only securing their Premier League status with two games remaining and exiting the League Cup to lower league opposition in a season that saw manager David Moyes come under pressure.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-138)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-139) In January 2023, Mark Noble returned to the club as sporting director.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-NobleDirector-140) Despite the troubles in West Ham's domestic campaign, they excelled in the Europa Conference League. The club progressed to the [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_UEFA_Europa_Conference_League_final "2023 UEFA Europa Conference League final") unbeaten, winning 13 games and drawing just once.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-141) They went on to win the competition, defeating [Fiorentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACF_Fiorentina "ACF Fiorentina") 2–1 in the final to claim their first major trophy since 1980 and their first European trophy in 58 years.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-142)

### Moyes departure, managerial changes, and relegation (2023–present)

Despite having led West Ham to three consecutive European seasons for the first time in their history, reaching at least the quarter-finals of each and culminating in the 2023 success, Moyes was not offered a new contract.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-143)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-144) On 23 May 2024, the club named [Julen Lopetegui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julen_Lopetegui "Julen Lopetegui") as his replacement.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-145) However Lopetegui would be sacked on 8 January 2025 with the team in 14th position, seven points above the relegation positions; during his tenure, they lost nine of 20 Premier League games.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-146)

On 9 January [Graham Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Potter "Graham Potter") was appointed as head coach signing a two–and–a–half year contract.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-147) This lasted until 27 September 2025 when Potter was sacked following poor results and performances over the second half of the [2024–25 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_Premier_League "2024–25 Premier League") and the start of the [2025–26 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025-26_Premier_League "2025-26 Premier League").[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-148)[Nuno Espírito Santo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuno_Esp%C3%ADrito_Santo "Nuno Espírito Santo") was appointed to take charge of the team, with West Ham 19th in the league.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-149)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-150)

By January 2026, Nuno's own managership was under question as they hit bottom three.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-151)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-152) After a stronger March and April which found them battling with Tottenham Hotspur and Nottingham Forest around the relegation zone, West Ham's defeat to Newcastle United on 17 May left them needing other results to go their way to avoid the drop.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-153) Despite a 3–0 win on the final day of the [2025–26 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_West_Ham_United_F.C._season "2025–26 West Ham United F.C. season") at home to Leeds United, relegation rivals Tottenham Hotspur won against Everton, relegating West Ham.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-154)
