### Thames Ironworks FC

The Thames Ironworks Team (1895–1900) used the [Union Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Flag "Union Flag") as its badge.

### Rivet Hammers

The principal element of the badge is the crossed pair of [rivet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivet "Rivet") hammers, tools that were used in the shipbuilding industry. The [Blackwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackwall,_London "Blackwall, London") and [Canning Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canning_Town "Canning Town") neighbourhoods surrounding the [Thames Ironworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Ironworks_and_Shipbuilding_Company "Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company") echoed to the sound of hammers; [steam hammers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_hammer "Steam hammer"), sledge hammers and rivet hammers.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-157)

Seven large mechanical steam hammers would punch small holes near the edges of the iron plates which would be joined to build the ships. The plates would be put in place and fixed together with rivets by teams of five, three inside the emerging vessel and two outside. Inside the ship one member of the team would heat the rivets till they were white hot and, using _Iron Fingers_ ([blacksmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacksmith "Blacksmith")'s [tongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongs "Tongs")), throw them to a second person, known as a "catch-boy" or "putter-in", who would pick the rivet up and place it the hole, also using tongs. The third person was known as the "holder-on" and he would then smash the rivet home with a sixteen-pound sledgehammer and then use his sledgehammer to hold the rivet in place while the men on the other side flattened the other end of the rivet.

Outside the ship, exposed to the elements, two men with rivet hammers – one right-handed, one left-handed – would hammer the protruding and still glowing rivet flat, so securing one of the many points necessary to link each of the ship's large plates. The crossed hammers were also incorporated into the coat of arms of the [County Borough of West Ham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Borough_of_West_Ham "County Borough of West Ham") and those of its successor, the modern [London Borough of Newham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Newham "London Borough of Newham").[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-158) The Thames Ironworks lay partly within what is now the London Borough of Tower Hamlets. However, the blacksmith's tongs in [that Borough's coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Tower_Hamlets#Coat_of_arms "London Borough of Tower Hamlets") represent the local saint, [Dunstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunstan "Dunstan"), the patron saint of [Stepney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stepney "Stepney") and metalworkers,[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-159) rather than the Ironworks.

### Tower

A yellow or white tower was added, intermittently, from the 1950s onwards.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-160) The primary reason for this seems to be to represent _Anne Boleyn's Tower_, the most notable feature of [Green Street House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Street_House "Green Street House"), an originally Tudor group of buildings which stood next to the [Boleyn Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boleyn_Ground "Boleyn Ground") until demolished in 1955. [Green Street House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Street_House "Green Street House") was also known as _Boleyn Castle_ through an association with [Anne Boleyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Boleyn "Anne Boleyn"). The manor was reputedly one of the sites at which [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") courted his second queen, though there is no documentary evidence to support the tradition.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-161) There are a number of other factors which may have influenced the inclusion of the stylised castle feature, for instance:

*   to reflect the contribution made to the club by players of [Old Castle Swifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Castle_Swifts "Old Castle Swifts")
*   The imposing towers, roofs and doorway of the Engineering Department of the [Thames Ironworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Ironworks_and_Shipbuilding_Company "Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company") bore a strong resemblance[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-162) to the castle feature in earlier iterations of the badge.
*   The first verse of the club's anthem, "[I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Forever_Blowing_Bubbles "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles")", begins "I'm dreaming dreams, I'm scheming schemes, I'm building castles high".
*   The [White Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Tower_(Tower_of_London) "White Tower (Tower of London)") of the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London") as emblematic of [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London "East London"). For hundreds of years, up until 1900, inner [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London "East London") had been known as the [Tower Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_division "Tower division"),[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-163) an area which owed military service to the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London"). The (originally whitewashed) [White Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Tower_(Tower_of_London) "White Tower (Tower of London)") was used as insignia for the area, for instance on cap badges of local units of the army.
*   In recognition of the ['West Ham Pals', the 13th Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham#First_World_War_%E2%80%93_West_Ham_Pals "West Ham") of the [Essex Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex_Regiment "Essex Regiment") which was raised in [Stratford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratford,_London "Stratford, London") in 1915 and saw extensive action and heavy losses on the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I) "Western Front (World War I)") in the [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). The Battalion was formed from volunteers from [West Ham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham "West Ham") and [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London "East London") generally. Their [war cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_cry "Battle cry") was "Up the Hammers". The cap badge of the [Essex Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex_Regiment "Essex Regiment") was the castle and key of Gibraltar, though the unit made an unsuccessful request to the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office") that crossed hammers could be used instead.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-164)
*   The adoption (in 1904) of Boleyn Castle FC[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-165) as the club's reserve side when they took over their grounds on the site.

### Shield

A shield has been used in many iterations of the club badge, and the shape of the 2016 version matches the cross-section on the hull of [HMS Warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Warrior_(1860) "HMS Warrior (1860)"), the most famous ship built by the Thames Ironworks.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Ham_United_F.C.#cite_note-166)

### Iterations

The crest was redesigned and updated in the late 1990s, featuring a wider yellow castle with fewer cruciform "windows" along with the peaked roofs being removed; the tops of the towers had previously made the castle appear more akin to [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland_Park_(Anaheim) "Disneyland Park (Anaheim)")'s Sleeping Beauty's Castle than a functioning fortress.
